issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of land for a company under the company-acquisition procedure is permissible for a work only when the work itself is directly useful to the public and the agreement secures public use of the work, rather than merely access for business with the company.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a company to construct a textile machinery parts factory, and the company was to pay the entire compensation.
The factory’s products were said to be useful to the public, but the factory itself was not available for direct public use.
The agreement provided only for access to and use of the land or works as necessary for the public to transact business with the company.
issues.conclusion: The factory’s useful products and the public’s limited business access did not satisfy the statutory requirements; the acquisition notification and resulting proceedings were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 40(1)(b) and 41, read together and in the context of sections 39 and 42 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, require the work itself to be directly useful to the public and the agreement to provide for public use of that work as such. The Court relied on Baba Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay for the restricted purposes permitted for company acquisitions, and distinguished the public-funded acquisition in Pandit Jhandu Lal v. State of Punjab. The public usefulness of a company’s product alone is insufficient.

rule.if: company_land_acquisition and company_pays_entire_compensation and work_not_directly_usable_by_public and public_access_only_for_business

predicates.company_land_acquisition: The government acquired land for a company through a compulsory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.company_pays_entire_compensation: The company was to bear the entire compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.work_not_directly_usable_by_public: The work constructed on the acquired land was not itself available for direct use by the public.
predicates.public_access_only_for_business: The agreement allowed members of the public to access or use the work only as needed to transact business with the company.

issues.definition: When land is compulsorily acquired for a company at its expense and the work is not directly usable by the public, business-related access alone results in an invalid company acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: The government’s satisfaction and a conclusive acquisition declaration do not prevent a court from deciding whether the proposed work and agreement meet the legal requirements for acquisition for a company.
material_facts: The government treated the factory’s products being useful to the public and business-related public access to the factory as sufficient to approve the acquisition.
The land was declared needed for the company, and the challenge concerned whether the proposed acquisition and agreement fell within the governing statutory requirements.
issues.conclusion: The court had jurisdiction to interpret the statutory requirements and determine whether they were met; the government’s satisfaction based on an incorrect interpretation did not validate the acquisition, and the declaration’s conclusiveness did not resolve that question.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 40(1)(b) and 41 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, require the court to determine the meaning of the statutory terms, while the government decides whether the facts satisfy those terms. Section 6(3) makes the declaration conclusive evidence that the land is needed for the stated purpose or company, but does not foreclose review of whether the acquisition satisfies the statutory conditions. The Court rejected the contrary implication of Ezra v. Secretary of State on the question before it.

predicates.company_land_acquisition: The government undertook a compulsory acquisition of land for a company.
predicates.government_satisfaction_based_on_broad_l: The government approved the acquisition on an interpretation that treated indirect public benefit or business-related access as sufficient.
predicates.statutory_conditions_challenged: A person affected by the acquisition challenged whether the proposed work or agreement met the legal conditions for that kind of acquisition.

issues.definition: When statutory compliance is challenged in a company land-acquisition proceeding, government satisfaction based on a broad interpretation does not prevent a court from reviewing whether the legal conditions were met.

issues.legal_issue: The company-acquisition procedure applies when the company bears the entire acquisition cost, while an acquisition primarily for a company may proceed as a public-purpose acquisition if acquisition costs are paid wholly or partly from public funds.
material_facts: The acquisition was for a company, and the company was to pay the entire compensation.
The government did not claim that any part of the compensation would be paid from public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority.
issues.conclusion: Because the company was to pay the entire compensation, the company-acquisition procedure applied and its conditions had to be satisfied.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 6(1), 39 and Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, distinguish company acquisitions from public-purpose acquisitions for which compensation is paid wholly or partly from public funds. The Court relied on Pandit Jhandu Lal v. State of Punjab for the proposition that a company-related acquisition with public funding may proceed as a public-purpose acquisition without the Part VII procedure.

predicates.company_land_acquisition: The government acquired land for the benefit or use of a company.
predicates.company_pays_entire_compensation: The company was to bear all compensation for the acquired land, with no contribution from public funds.

issues.definition: A company-funded compulsory acquisition of land must proceed under the procedure applicable to acquisitions for companies.
